 Serving Indianapolis and the Northside communities listed on this site.

 Storm preparation around the home
 Four practical places to start before the next downpour.

 01
 Test the whole sump-pump cycle

 When conditions are dry and it is safe, confirm that the float starts the pump, the water level drops, and water leaves through the discharge point.

 02
 Keep discharge water away

 A line that ends too close to the foundation, leaks, freezes shut, or sends water toward a low spot can bring it right back.

 03
 Check the water coming from above

 Clear gutters, repair obvious leaks, and make sure downspouts and surface grading carry roof water away from the house.

 04
 Plan for the failure point

 Power loss, a stuck float, return flow, a blocked line, and sewer backup can all defeat an otherwise working system. Ask which safeguards fit your home.

 Before you call.

 A few of the questions we hear most. If yours isn't here, the phone is the fastest way through.

 How fast can you get out here?

 Are you licensed and insured in Indiana?

 David Kropczynski holds an active Indiana Plumbing Contractor credential. Indiana licenses: Plumbing Contractor PC12300114 (David Kropczynski); Plumbing Corporation CO52600043 (Simple Man Plumbing). Ask about the documentation and scope that apply to your specific project.

 Do you give an upfront price before you start?

 We explain the work and provide clear pricing before you decide how to proceed. Ask for the current estimate for your repair or installation.

 How do payment options work?

 We accept all major credit and debit cards (Visa, Mastercard, Amex, Discover), ACH transfers, and personal checks upon completion. For larger installations and staged projects, milestone payment terms can be written directly into the proposal.

 Can I call about an urgent water problem?

 Call to discuss current availability for an urgent leak, water intrusion, sewer backup, or no-water issue.

 What warranty terms apply?

 Every job carries a one-year workmanship guarantee. If something we installed or repaired fails because of how the work was done, we come back and make it right at no additional labor charge. Manufacturer warranties on parts and fixtures are separate and vary by product - ask and we'll tell you what applies to yours.

 Home  /  About

 A Practice, Not a Production Line
 About Simple Man.

 We treat every visit like it's our own house - because most of our calls come from neighbors who saw the truck on the next street over.

 An Introduction
 Dave. Owner.

 On the tools for over eight years. Still answering the phone, still writing up every job by hand before leaving the driveway.

 I started this practice because I couldn't find a plumber who treated my mother's house the way I'd treat my own. Twenty-some years on, the standard hasn't moved: show up when I say I will, explain what I'm doing in language a homeowner actually understands, leave the space cleaner than I found it.

 If we're working in your home, you'll have my cell number before I leave. That's the simplest way I know to mean what I say.

 - Dave

 Owner & Lead Plumber · Indiana Plumbing Contractor

 Years of hands-on work.

 Built one job at a time, on the Northside and across greater Indianapolis.

 The Story
 Doing things the right way - the simple way.

 At Simple Man Plumbing, we believe in doing things the right way - the simple way. With years of hands-on experience in residential plumbing, we've built a reputation for being reliable, transparent, and always on time. From fixing leaky faucets to full-scale plumbing installations, we've done it all.

 The name says most of what we believe. We are simple men doing honest work. We don't pad invoices, we don't invent problems, and we don't leave a job until you'd be glad to have us back.

 Our service area runs from Greenwood up through downtown Indianapolis and into the Northside - Carmel, Fishers, Westfield, Noblesville, and out east to Pendleton. The size of the job changes; the standard does not.

 I. On Time, Always
 If we're running late, you'll hear it from us before the window closes.

 II. No Hidden Costs
 We quote what it takes. If something changes, we stop and ask first.

 III. Clean Work Sites
 Drop cloths down, dust contained, mess hauled out.

 IV. Done Right, Or It's On Us
 Every job carries a one-year workmanship guarantee. If our work fails, we come back and make it right.

 A Considered Workflow
 How a typical job runs.

 Step · 01 First call
 You ring. We listen. We ask the questions a plumber would ask, schedule a visit, and tell you who's coming.

 Step · 02 On site
 We diagnose before we wrench. We walk the system, identify root cause, and explain it in plain language.

 Step · 03 The work
 Done to code, with the right materials, and we leave the space cleaner than we found it. Pictures and notes for your file.

 Step · 04 Clear terms
 Before work begins, ask about the scope, pricing, and warranty terms for your specific project.

 Home  /  Flood Prevention & Sump Pumps

 Last updated: August 17, 2026

 Before the next heavy rain
 Flood prevention & sump pumps in Indianapolis, IN.

 A practical guide to sump pumps, backup power, discharge routing, drainage coordination, and flood-prevention plumbing for Indianapolis-area homeowners.

 Start with the system One pump,
 many failure points.

 A basement can take on water even when the pump itself is working. Before replacing equipment, look at where water enters, how it reaches the basin, whether the pump can cycle freely, and where the discharge ends up.

 01 · Collection
 Pit & basin
 The basin needs to collect water without a blocked inlet, loose cover, or float that cannot move.

 02 · Pumping
 Pump & float
 The pump must lift water reliably, and the float must start it before water reaches a damaging level.

 03 · Sending
 Check valve & pipe
 A check valve helps keep discharged water from dropping back into the pit when the pump stops.

 04 · Releasing
 Discharge route
 Water needs a lawful, practical route away from the foundation and away from places it can return.

 01
 Sump pump work
 Install, replace,
 test before trouble.

 A pump that is noisy, cycling too often, failing to start, or running without lowering the water level deserves attention before the next storm. The right answer may be a repair, a replacement, a pit correction, or a discharge correction-not automatically a bigger pump.

 Installation or replacement Match the pump to the pit and lift

 Seasonal testing Float · pump · discharge

 Basin and pit review Capacity · cover · access

 Check valve review Limit return flow

 A simple homeowner check
 Watch the whole cycle.

 When conditions are dry and it is safe to do so, add water to the pit slowly enough to see the float rise. Confirm that the pump starts, the water level drops, and water leaves from the discharge point. Do not handle a pump, cord, outlet, or panel if any electrical component is wet or compromised.

 If the pump hums without moving water, trips power, runs continuously, or the pit rises toward overflow, stop testing and get help.

 02
 Power & discharge
 Plan for the rain
 and the outage.

 The moment a sump system is needed most can coincide with a power interruption. Battery backup systems are one option worth discussing, but their fit, runtime, and installation requirements depend on the specific pump and home.

 Battery backup conversation Capacity · load · runtime

 Discharge pipe routing Move water away from the foundation

 Freeze and blockage risk Keep the line inspectable

 Check valve placement Reduce water falling back

 The route matters
 Water should not come home again.

 A discharge that ends too close to the house, leaks beside the foundation, freezes shut, or aims toward a low spot can undermine a good pump. The route also needs to respect property lines and local requirements.

 If runoff is pooling near the house, the solution may involve grading, extensions, downspout routing, or drainage work outside the pit. A plumbing visit can help identify which questions belong to the plumber and which belong to a drainage, foundation, or landscape professional.

 Prevention around the home A dry basement starts outside the basement.

 01 Gutters & downspouts
 Keep gutters clear, repair obvious leaks, and make sure downspouts carry roof water away instead of dumping it at the foundation.

 02 Grade & surface flow
 Observe where water gathers after a hard rain. Low areas beside the house, settled soil, and failed splash blocks can send surface water toward the structure.

 03 Basement plumbing
 For homes vulnerable to sewer backups, ask about whether a backwater valve is appropriate. It is not a universal add-on: the piping layout and local code matter.

 04 Routine preparation
 Keep the sump-pit area accessible. Know where the electrical panel and main water shutoff are, and avoid storing valuables directly on a basement floor.

 Make a useful service call The details that help a plumber diagnose faster.

 I. What changed?
 Was this the first time? Did the pump run constantly, stop running, or lose power? Did water arrive after rain, a sewer backup, or a plumbing leak?

 II. Where is the water?
 Note whether it is in the pit, along a wall, near a floor drain, around a fixture, or coming from overhead plumbing.

 III. Where does it go?
 If safe, identify the discharge outlet and whether water is visible there when the pump runs. A photo from a dry, safe location can help.

 IV. What has been tried?
 Share recent repairs, previous flooding, unusual sounds, breaker trips, or changes to landscaping, gutters, and downspouts.

 Safety first When it is more than a plumbing call.
 A plumber can help with a sump system and many home plumbing conditions. Electrical hazards, fast-rising water, gas odors, and threats to people need a different first response.

 What if water is close to outlets, a panel, or electrical equipment?
 Do not enter standing water or touch electrical equipment when a shock hazard may exist. If it is safe to do so from a dry location, keep people away from the area. Contact the appropriate emergency or utility resource before any plumbing work is attempted.

 What if I smell gas?
 Leave the area, avoid switches, flames, and anything that could ignite gas, and contact the gas utility or emergency services from a safe location. Do not treat a gas odor as a sump-pump issue.

 Can I use a portable pump or shop vacuum?
 Only when the setup is appropriate and there is no electrical hazard. Do not use ordinary household equipment in unsafe standing water, and do not rely on it as a substitute for professional emergency response when water is rising or affecting utilities. For an already-flooded basement, follow official safety guidance; pumping out a flooded basement too quickly can create structural risk.

 Should I add a backwater valve?
 A backwater valve can be relevant for some homes with sewer-backup risk, but it must be chosen for the actual pipe layout and installed in a way that remains accessible for service. Ask for a site-specific evaluation rather than treating it as a standard fix.

 For household flood safety and recovery information, see the Indiana Department of Homeland Security flood-safety guidance and FEMA's homeowner flood guide .

you can see right now.

 Home  /  Service Areas  /  Broad Ripple

 Marion County · Same-day
 Plumbing in Broad Ripple.

 Charm, character, and a hundred years of plumbing history hidden behind plaster. Broad Ripple’s older homes hold surprises in the walls — we’ve seen most of them, and we know how to work without tearing the place apart.

 Serving Broad Ripple · the Northside

 On the Ground in Broad Ripple
 What we actually see in Broad Ripple homes.

 Broad Ripple is one of the oldest village neighborhoods on the Northside, built up in the 1910s and 20s along the Monon and the Central Canal. The 1920s bungalows and cottages that give it its charm also hide a century of plumbing behind their plaster — and we’ve been into most of it.

 These homes were plumbed in galvanized steel and drained through cast iron, and after a hundred years both are usually due. Tight lots and original walls mean replacements have to be done carefully and cleanly; we route new copper or PEX with as little demolition as the house will allow.

 Proximity to the White River and the canal means some Broad Ripple basements take on water, so sump pumps and proper drainage are a recurring theme. The mature trees lining the old streets send roots straight into clay sewer laterals — a backed-up main is a classic Broad Ripple call, especially after a wet spring.

 Where we work in Broad Ripple

 Flood readiness
 Flood prevention and sump-pump help in Broad Ripple.

 Near the White River and canal, a wet basement can start with more than one problem. We can look at the sump system, the discharge route, and the sewer lateral together so a heavy-rain plan fits the house instead of treating one symptom.

 That can mean sump-pump testing before storm season, replacing an aging pump, discussing a backup system, or evaluating whether a sewer backup or backwater valve concern needs attention. The goal is practical drainage and flood-prevention work for the way older Broad Ripple homes are built.

 Hamilton County · By appointment
 Plumbing in Carmel.

 From the Village of WestClay to the older streets near the Monon, Carmel’s mix of high-end new builds and established homes each bring their own plumbing demands. We know the neighborhoods, the water table, and the standard of finish Carmel expects.

 Call (765) 860-8667 &rarr;

 8+ yrs
 Of hands-on plumbing experience

 1-yr
 Workmanship guarantee on every job

 Upfront
 Pricing and scope agreed in writing before work begins

 Serving Carmel · the Northside

 On the Ground in Carmel
 What we actually see in Carmel homes.

 Carmel splits cleanly into two plumbing worlds. There’s Old Town and the streets near the Monon — older, established, smaller homes — and then the sprawling 1990s-to-now construction out toward the Village of WestClay, Bridgewater, and the roundabout-laced north side.

 That timeline matters. A lot of Carmel’s 1980s and 90s homes were plumbed with polybutylene (gray poly) supply line, which fails at the fittings and is worth getting ahead of before it lets go inside a finished basement. Newer builds run PEX and are generally sound, but big homes mean long runs, recirculation loops, and more than one water heater to keep balanced.

 Carmel sits on the same hard Central Indiana water as the rest of Hamilton County, so softeners and scale management are routine here. Clay soil and finished lower levels also make a reliable sump pump — ideally with a battery backup — close to non-negotiable for most homes.

 Where we work in Carmel

 Old Town Carmel

 Bridgewater

 Brookshire

 Common local calls

 Polybutylene supply line in 80s–90s homes

 Recirculation & multiple water heaters in larger homes

 Hard-water scale and softener service

 Sump pump + battery backup for finished basements

 Flood readiness
 Flood prevention and sump-pump help in Carmel.

 Finished lower levels and clay soil make flood prevention part of routine home care in Carmel. A visit can start with a sump-pump test, then follow the discharge line outside to make sure water is moving away from the foundation.

 Before a heavy rain, we can discuss backup-system options, replace a pump that is near the end of its service life, and evaluate wet-basement, sewer-backup, or backwater-valve concerns. That gives a Carmel homeowner a clearer plan before water is at the door.

 On the Ground in Castleton
 What we actually see in Castleton homes.

 Castleton grew up around the mall in the 1970s and 80s, and the subdivisions, condos, and apartments filling the area largely date from that same stretch. Its position on the Northside, right off I-69, makes us quick to respond — which matters most in a deep freeze.

 Homes from that era are now at the age where original systems give out: builder water heaters well past their warranty, aging cast-iron and ABS drains, and — in some early-80s builds — polybutylene supply line living on borrowed time. It’s a neighborhood where getting ahead of a replacement saves a lot of grief.

 Quick access up I-69 and across the Northside means rapid response for repairs, which is exactly what you want during a winter pressure event when a frozen line lets go. Hard Central Indiana water keeps water heaters and fixtures scaling right on schedule.

 Serving Fishers · the Northside

 On the Ground in Fishers
 What we actually see in Fishers homes.

 Fishers grew up fast and grew up recently — most of what we work on was built from the 1990s onward, from the Nickel Plate District out to the lakefront homes ringing Geist Reservoir. It’s newer construction, which brings its own particular set of surprises.

 ‘Newer’ doesn’t mean trouble-free. The earliest Fishers subdivisions caught the tail end of polybutylene pipe, and the builder-grade water heaters and fixtures from the 2000s are now reaching the age where they start to fail. We work clean around finished basements, hardwood, and fresh tile — the standard a newer home expects.

 Anywhere near Geist the water table runs high, so sump pumps do real work and a backup pump earns its keep every spring. Hard water is a given across Hamilton County, and lake-area homes often run softeners and whole-home filtration that we service and dial in.

 Home  /  Service Areas  /  Indianapolis

 Marion County · Same-day where possible
 Plumbing in Indianapolis.

 Indianapolis is where Simple Man Plumbing lives and works. From Northside bungalows to downtown lofts and post-war ranches, we know the city’s housing stock, its old galvanized lines, and the quirks that come with a century of additions.

 Call (765) 860-8667 &rarr;
 Book a Indianapolis visit &rarr;

 8+ yrs
 Of hands-on plumbing experience

 1-yr
 Workmanship guarantee on every job

 Upfront
 Pricing and scope agreed in writing before work begins

 Serving Indianapolis · the Northside

 On the Ground in Indianapolis
 What we actually see in Indianapolis homes.

 Indianapolis is a city of old housing stock, and old housing stock is where plumbing gets interesting. Inside I-465 you’ll find Craftsman bungalows in Irvington and Meridian-Kessler, double-brick homes in Fountain Square, and converted lofts downtown — most of them pushing or past a century old.

 In pre-1960 homes we routinely find original galvanized-steel supply lines, corroded nearly shut from the inside, and cast-iron drains on the back half of their life. Clay sewer laterals running out to the street are the other constant — mature trees and root intrusion go hand in hand around here, and a backed-up main is one of our most common Indy calls.

 Marion County is served by Citizens Energy Group, and the older core still runs a combined storm-and-sanitary sewer — which is why a hard rain can push water back into low basements until the DigIndy tunnels finish their work. Add hard Central Indiana water that scales out water heaters early, and there’s always something to stay ahead of.

 Where we work in Indianapolis

 Irvington
 Meridian-Kessler
 Fountain Square
 Broad Ripple
 Butler-Tarkington
 Lockerbie Square
 Downtown / Mile Square

 Common local calls

 Galvanized & cast-iron replacement in pre-war homes

 Clay sewer laterals with tree-root intrusion

 Combined-sewer basement backups in heavy rain

 Hard-water scale in aging water heaters

 The Practice
 Plumbing services in Indianapolis.

 01
 Residential Plumbing

 Expert plumbing from the ground up - new installs, repipes, additions. The kind of careful work that disappears once the wall is closed.

 Open the spec &rarr;

 02
 Everyday Repairs

 Reliable fixes for life's plumbing hiccups - leaks, clogs, running toilets, sump pumps. The small failures that quietly turn a household upside down.

 Open the spec &rarr;

 03
 System Upgrades

 Modern solutions for a more efficient home - tank and tankless water heaters, soft-water systems, pressure regulators, and long-life fixtures.

 Open the spec &rarr;

 Flood readiness
 Flood prevention and sump-pump help in Indianapolis.

 In older Indianapolis neighborhoods, heavy rain can stress both a lower-level sump system and an aging sewer lateral. We can test or replace a sump pump, review its discharge routing, and help sort out whether water in a basement points to drainage, a backup, or both.

 For homes affected by combined-sewer conditions, a flood-prevention visit can include backup-system discussion and a backwater-valve evaluation. It is a practical way to prepare before the next storm instead of guessing after water shows up.

 Serving Keystone at the Crossing · the Northside

 On the Ground in Keystone at the Crossing
 What we actually see in Keystone at the Crossing homes.

 Keystone at the Crossing is the Northside’s upscale core — the Fashion Mall, the Village of Keystone, and a dense mix of mid-rise condos, townhomes, and luxury residences, with the old-money estates of Williams Creek just to the west. Plumbing here is as much about coordination as it is about pipe.

 In condos and townhomes, work means shared stacks, common-wall shutoffs, and HOA-grade documentation — you can’t just kill the water to a whole building on a whim, so we plan the shutoff, protect finishes, and paper every visit. In the higher-end single-family homes it’s premium fixtures, recirculation systems, and finish work that has to look right the first time.

 Mid-rise and multi-unit buildings carry their own pressure-balancing and water-heater logistics, and associations expect a clear written record of what was done. Hard water still runs through all of it, so softening and scale control stay part of the conversation.

 Serving Noblesville · the Northside

 On the Ground in Noblesville
 What we actually see in Noblesville homes.

 Noblesville carries more history than its Hamilton County neighbors. The Victorian-era homes ringing the downtown courthouse square are genuinely old, while the east side and the Morse Reservoir shoreline bring decades of newer development — and we carry parts for both on every truck.

 Around the square, expect the full pre-war menu: galvanized supply, cast-iron stacks, and the occasional surprise left behind by a century of remodels. Out by Morse and the newer additions it’s PEX and modern fixtures, where the work is more about water heaters, softeners, and lakefront sump systems than wholesale replacement.

 Lakefront and low-lying lots near Morse Reservoir sit on a high water table, so sump pumps and battery backups matter here. Rural pockets still run on private wells, and the region’s hard water keeps softeners busy on both the old and new sides of town.

 Plumbing in Pendleton.

 Serving Pendleton · the Northside

 On the Ground in Pendleton
 What we actually see in Pendleton homes.

 Pendleton sits out east in Madison County, where the historic town center around Falls Park gives way quickly to rural properties on acreage. On a single road you might find one home on municipal service and the next on a private well — and we’re set up for both.

 The older homes near downtown carry the usual century-old mix of galvanized and cast iron, while the country properties run well pumps, pressure tanks, and the softeners that very hard well water demands out here. Septic systems are common too, which shapes how we approach drains and fixtures on the rural side.

 Well water in this part of Madison County is notably hard and often iron-heavy, so softeners and filtration aren’t a luxury — they’re what keeps the fixtures and water heater alive. We service the whole well side of the system: pumps, pressure tanks, switches, and treatment.

 Where we work in Pendleton

 Serving Westfield · the Northside

 On the Ground in Westfield
 What we actually see in Westfield homes.

 Westfield is the fastest-growing piece of the map, anchored by Grand Park and filling in with new subdivisions almost faster than the roads keep up — Chatham Hills, Maple Knoll, and the corridors around US-31. Most of our calls here are on homes still settling into their first decade.

 New construction has a predictable rhythm: rough-in work, then first-year warranty calls as a house settles and the punch-list surfaces — a weeping shutoff, a poorly pitched drain, a water heater that was never quite right. We handle both ends, and we’ll gladly give a builder’s plumbing a second look before your warranty runs out.

 Parts of greater Westfield only recently moved off private wells and septic onto municipal service, so we still see pressure tanks and softeners on the older, more rural edges. Hard water, clay soil, and the usual Central Indiana freeze risk round out what we plan for.

 Plumbing in Zionsville.

 Zionsville is more than its brick Main Street. The historic Village, newer communities along the US 421 corridor, and rural properties across the former township lands each come with a different water, sewer, and drainage picture.

 Serving Zionsville · the Northside

 On the Ground in Zionsville
 What we actually see in Zionsville homes.

 Zionsville grew from an 1850s rail village into a town that now spans historic, suburban, and rural settings. Around the brick streets of the Village, older homes call for careful work around existing finishes and aging service lines. Farther out, planned neighborhoods such as Stonegate and Holliday Farms bring larger systems, finished lower levels, irrigation, and higher-capacity hot-water demand.

 The rural service district changes the job again. Citizens Water serves most of the urban district, Whitestown serves portions of the west, and some northern and western properties rely on private wells. Wastewater service also changes by address among the Town, TriCo, and Whitestown, so we verify the utility territory before planning sewer or service-line work instead of assuming every Zionsville home is connected the same way.

 Citizens describes Central Indiana water as very hard — about 19 grains per gallon on average — so scale control, softener settings, and water-heater maintenance matter here. Around Eagle Creek and its tributaries, floodplain and stormwater conditions also make sump capacity, backup power, and discharge routing worth evaluating, especially when a lower level is finished.

 Flood readiness
 Flood prevention and sump-pump help in Zionsville.

 Near Eagle Creek and its tributaries, a property’s drainage and sump capacity are worth reviewing before sustained rain arrives. We can test a sump pump, replace a failing unit, and check whether the discharge route is carrying water safely away from the home.

 For a finished lower level, we can discuss backup systems and evaluate wet-basement, sewer-backup, or backwater-valve concerns. That gives Zionsville homeowners a practical flood-prevention plan that accounts for the property, not just the weather forecast.

 Explore flood & sump-pump help &rarr;

 Sump-pump testing, installation & replacement

 Backup-system options for lower levels

 The Common Questions
 Before you call.

 A few of the questions we hear most from Zionsville homeowners. If yours isn't here, the phone is the fastest way through.

 How fast can you get to Zionsville?

 Call to discuss current availability. For active leaks, water intrusion, sewer backup, or no-water, tell us when you call so we can understand the urgency.

 Are you licensed and insured in Indiana?

 David Kropczynski holds an active Indiana Plumbing Contractor credential. Indiana licenses: Plumbing Contractor PC12300114 (David Kropczynski); Plumbing Corporation CO52600043 (Simple Man Plumbing). Ask about the documentation and scope that apply to your specific project.

 Do you give an upfront price before you start?

 We explain the work and provide clear pricing before you decide how to proceed. Ask for the current estimate for your repair or installation.

 How do payment options work?

 We accept all major credit and debit cards (Visa, Mastercard, Amex, Discover), ACH transfers, and personal checks upon completion. For larger installations and staged projects, milestone payment terms can be written directly into the proposal.

 Can I call about an urgent water problem in Zionsville?

 Call to discuss current availability for an urgent leak, water intrusion, sewer backup, or no-water issue.

 What warranty terms apply?

 Every job carries a one-year workmanship guarantee. If something we installed or repaired fails because of how the work was done, we come back and make it right at no additional labor charge. Manufacturer warranties on parts and fixtures are separate and vary by product - ask and we'll tell you what applies to yours.
